source_text: Sit autem orantibus sermo et precatio cum disciplina quietem continens et pudorem. cogitemus nos sub conspectu Dei stare. placendum est diuinis oculis et habitu corporis et modo uocis. nam ut inpudentis est clamoribus strepere, ita contra congruit uerecundo modestis precibus orare. denique magisterio suo Dominus secrete orare nos praecepit, in abditis et semotis locis, in cubiculis ipsis, quod magis conuenit fidei, ut sciamus Deum ubique esse praesentem, audire omnes et uidere et maiestatis suae plenitudine in abdita quoque et occulta penetrare, sicut scriptum est: ego Deus adproximans et non Deus de longinquo. si absconditus fuerit homo in absconditis, ego ergo non uidebo eum? nonne caelum et terram ego inpleo? et iterum: in omni loco oculi Dei speculantur bonos et malos. et quando in unum cum fratribus conuenimus et sacrificia diuina cum Dei sacerdote celebramus, uerecundiae et disciplinae memores esse debemus, non passim uentilare preces nostras inconditis uocibus nec petitionem commendandam modeste Deo tumultuosa loquacitate iactare quia Deus non uocis sed cordis auditor est, nec admonendus est clamoribus qui cogitationes uidet probante Domino et dicente: quid cogitatis nequam in cordi bus uestris ? et alio loco: et scient omnes ecclesiae quia ego sum scrutator renis et cordis.
thought_title: Prayer must be quiet, modest, and mindful of God's presence
orientation: Cyprian is teaching how Christians should pray, now turning from the Lord's Prayer itself to the manner and disposition of prayer.
pass_a_gloss: But let the speech and prayer of those praying be with discipline, containing quietness and modesty. Let us think that we stand under the sight of God. We must please the divine eyes both by the bearing of the body and by the manner of the voice. For just as it is the mark of a shameless person to make a din with shoutings, so on the contrary it is fitting for a modest person to pray with restrained prayers. Finally, by his own teaching the Lord commanded us to pray in secret, in hidden and remote places, in the very bedchambers, which is more fitting for faith, so that we may know that God is present everywhere, that he hears and sees all things, and that by the fullness of his majesty he penetrates even hidden and secret places, as it is written: I am a God drawing near, and not a God from afar. If a man has hidden himself in hidden places, shall I then not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? And again: In every place the eyes of God watch the good and the evil. And when we come together in one place with the brothers and celebrate the divine sacrifices with the priest of God, we ought to be mindful of modesty and discipline, not to scatter our prayers here and there with unformed voices, nor to throw about with noisy talkativeness a petition that should be commended to God modestly, because God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart, and he does not need to be reminded by shoutings, since he sees the thoughts, as the Lord proves and says: Why do you think evil things in your hearts? And in another place: And all the churches shall know that I am the searcher of reins and heart.

choices.term: sermo et precatio cum disciplina quietem continens et pudorem
choices.english: speech and prayer with discipline, containing quietness and modesty
choices.why: Keeps the two nouns distinct and preserves the participial phrase as a quality of the prayer, matching the source's compactness.
rejected: the words and prayer of those praying should be disciplined, quiet, and modest

choices.english: stand under the sight of God
choices.why: Renders the spatial metaphor literally, emphasizing the awareness of God's watching presence.

choices.english: it is the mark of a shameless person to make a din with shoutings
choices.why: Preserves the genitive of characteristic and the noisy connotation of 'strepere'.
rejected: it is shameless to shout loudly

choices.english: for a modest person to pray with restrained prayers
choices.why: Keeps the dative of the person and the adjective 'modestis' modifying 'precibus', matching the source's parallel structure.
rejected: a modest person should pray quietly

choices.term: non passim uentilare preces nostras inconditis uocibus
choices.english: not to scatter our prayers here and there with unformed voices
choices.why: 'Ventilare' suggests tossing or scattering; 'inconditis' means unformed or disordered, so this keeps the image of careless, noisy prayer.
rejected: not to pour out our prayers with disorderly shouts

choices.why: 'Iactare' means to toss or fling about, and 'tumultuosa loquacitate' conveys noisy, disorderly speech; the rendering keeps the negative image.

pass_b_english: But when we pray, our speech and prayer should be disciplined, quiet, and modest. Let us remember that we are standing under the sight of God. We must please the divine eyes both by the posture of our body and by the tone of our voice. For just as it is the mark of a shameless person to make a din with shoutings, so it is fitting for a modest person to pray with restrained prayers. Finally, the Lord by his own teaching commanded us to pray in secret, in hidden and secluded places, in our very bedchambers. This is more in keeping with faith, so that we may know that God is present everywhere, that he hears and sees all things, and that in the fullness of his majesty he penetrates even hidden and secret places. As it is written: "I am a God who draws near, and not a God far off. If a person hides himself in secret places, will I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?" (Jeremiah 23:23-24). And again: "In every place the eyes of God watch the good and the evil" (Proverbs 15:3). And when we gather together with the brothers and celebrate the divine sacrifices with God's priest, we ought to remember modesty and discipline. We should not scatter our prayers here and there with unformed voices, nor throw about with noisy talkativeness a petition that should be commended to God with restraint. For God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart. He does not need to be prompted by shoutings, since he sees our thoughts, as the Lord proves when he says: "Why do you think evil in your hearts?" (Matthew 9:4). And in another place: "And all the churches will know that I am the one who searches minds and hearts" (Revelation 2:23).

last_rejected.source_quote: in omni loco oculi Dei speculantur bonos et malos
last_rejected.why: The Latin quote matches Jeremiah 23:24 LXX/Vulgate continuation, not Proverbs 15:3.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'in omni loco oculi Dei speculantur bonos et malos' matches Proverbs 15:3 Vulgate, not Jeremiah.

last_rejected.quote: as the Lord proves when he says: "Why do you think evil in your hearts?"
last_rejected.source_quote: probante Domino et dicente: quid cogitatis nequam in cordibus uestris
last_rejected.why: English hides that 'Domino' refers to Christ (the Lord), not God the Father; context is Matthew 9:4.
last_rejected.fix: as the Lord himself proves when he says...
last_rejected.ruling: 'the Lord' correctly renders 'Domino'; English doesn't hide Christ, and source doesn't specify Father either.

last_rejected.quote: "And all the churches will know that I am the one who searches minds and hearts" (Revelation 2:23)
last_rejected.source_quote: et scient omnes ecclesiae quia ego sum scrutator renis et cordis
last_rejected.why: English attributes this to Revelation, but source lacks speaker marking; this is Christ's voice in Revelation, yet Cyprian presents it as Scripture without specifying speaker.
last_rejected.fix: And all the churches shall know that I am the searcher of the reins and heart
last_rejected.ruling: Revelation 2:23 is correct source; adding speaker marking is a preference, not a meaning-changing error.
